title: America Just Added Its Fewest Jobs Since February. India’s IT Stocks Are Rallying.
excerpt: The U.S. economy created only 57,000 jobs in June — roughly half what Wall Street expected. The weak print has pushed back rate-hike fears, sent the dollar tumbling, and given Indian markets their strongest week in months.
body:
The American labour market just delivered its weakest showing since February, and the ripple effects are being felt from Wall Street to Dalal Street.

The U.S. economy added only 57,000 non-farm jobs in June, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Thursday — badly missing the 110,000 consensus forecast and snapping a three-month streak of surprising strength. Payroll gains for April and May were revised downward by a cumulative 74,000, painting an even softer picture of the hiring landscape.

The unemployment rate dipped to 4.2% from 4.3%, but the improvement was driven by people leaving the workforce rather than finding jobs. Leisure and hospitality — the sector many had expected would surge on the back of the FIFA World Cup — shed 61,000 positions, reflecting what economists called "weaker than usual seasonal hiring."

## Why India Is Cheering a Weak U.S. Jobs Print

For Indian markets, bad news in America is, counterintuitively, good news.

The soft report prompted traders to slash the probability of a Federal Reserve rate hike in September from roughly 75% to about 53%. The dollar index slid 0.5%, setting up its biggest weekly drop since early April. And lower U.S. rates mean cheaper capital flows into emerging markets — exactly the kind of tailwind India needs after months of foreign fund outflows.

Indian IT companies, which earn the bulk of their revenue in the United States, led the charge. The Nifty IT index jumped 1.9% at Friday's open, with HCLTech surging over 5% — compounding gains from its $1.14 billion deal with a major European firm announced the same day. The benchmark Nifty 50 rose 0.83% to 24,375, while the Sensex climbed 0.84% to 78,152.

"Two key headwinds have eased," said Todd McClone, portfolio manager at William Blair Investment Management. "India is among the most oversold markets we track."

## The Rupee Gets Room to Breathe

The Indian rupee, battered to near-record lows earlier this year, is expected to snap a four-day losing streak on Friday. Traders anticipate the currency opening in the 95.12–95.16 range, up from Thursday's close at 95.39. The rupee has already logged its first quarterly gain in five quarters, climbing back from the 97-per-dollar depths of May on the back of falling oil prices and the fragile Iran-U.S. peace deal.

Goldman Sachs has raised its 2026 growth forecast for India by 30 basis points and now expects a balance of payments surplus of 0.7% of GDP.

## The Broader Picture: A Labour Market in Transition

Despite the headline weakness, the U.S. labour market is not collapsing. Average monthly job gains totalled 111,000 over the past quarter — stronger than at any point in 2025. Initial jobless claims remain low at 215,000. The problem is not layoffs; it is a slowdown in new hiring.

"June payrolls point to a labour market settling into a lower gear, not one rolling over," wrote Jason Pride, chief of investment strategy at Glenmede.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, who has abandoned forward guidance since taking the helm, noted earlier this week that inflation expectations have declined in the past four weeks. But one report is unlikely to change the Fed's stance. Capital Economics wrote that "it will take a couple more underwhelming payrolls prints for the doves on the FOMC to have the more compelling argument."

## What This Means for NRIs and the Diaspora

For the estimated 4.8 million Indian Americans — many of whom work in the technology and professional services sectors that have been whipsawed by AI-driven restructuring and visa uncertainty — the cooling labour market is a double-edged sword.

On one hand, a less aggressive Fed means mortgage rates and borrowing costs could stabilise, offering relief to households stretched by two years of elevated interest rates. On the other, the slowdown in hiring, particularly in professional services which added just 36,000 jobs, signals that the white-collar job market remains competitive.

For those considering a return to India, the calculus is shifting. The rupee's stabilisation, India's outperformance against Asia's AI-driven correction, and a domestic economy that still grew at over 7% last fiscal year all tilt the equation. India's stock market recaptured the $5 trillion mark this week, foreign funds are trickling back, and oil prices have crashed to pre-war levels — erasing the one macro risk that kept global investors away.

The U.S. economy is not in trouble. But it is no longer the effortless job-creation machine that made staying in America feel like the obvious choice.
